title: International Right-Wing Network Behind Documentary Attacking Mexico’s Judicial Reform
author: Aníbal García Fernández
content:
_This article by[Aníbal García
Fernández](https://contralinea.com.mx/author/anibal/) originally appeared in
the [November 10, 2026 edition of
Contralínea](https://contralinea.com.mx/interno/semana/red-de-la-derecha-
internacional-detras-del-documental-cuando-perdimos-el-juicio/), a Mexican
investigative journalism magazine._

_Although the documentary titled “When We Lost Our Judgment” (“Cuando perdimos
el juicio”) was presented as a journalistic product, it is part of a series of
inputs generated by a network of the Mexican and international right that
seeks to plant the idea that Mexico is advancing toward authoritarianism,
without supposed institutional “checks and balances.” That is why its main
purpose is to question the judicial reform. Behind that product are several
organizations, some of them even allies of the NED; among them: Konrad
Adenauer Stiftung, Juicio Justo, the Due Process of Law Foundation, Réplica,
New York University’s Rule of Law._

The documentary titled “When We Lost Our Judgment,” which questions the
judicial reform in Mexico, was recently released. Behind it are **several non-
governmental organizations that are part of the large network of the Mexican
and international right** , among them: Juicio Justo, the Due Process of Law
Foundation, Réplica, New York University’s Rule of Law and the Konrad Adenauer
Stiftung.

![Poster for the presentation of the
documentary](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/2026-11-11-right-wing-network-
documentary-02-documentary-poster.jpg)Image: Contralínea

As on other occasions, those who attack the transformation in Mexico see in
the judicial reform one of the most questionable and critical processes. Even
opponents, national and foreign, have said that with this reform –and others–
democracy in Mexico is being eroded.

Nothing could be more false. On the contrary, it was the previous Supreme
Court of Justice of the Nation (SCJN) that was antidemocratic, the one chosen
by the “dedazo” of Ernesto Zedillo Ponce de León, the author of Fobaproa, of
the structural reforms, the privatizations, the highway bailout and the
indebtedness. The same president who did not know how to deal with the
situation in Chiapas and ended up violating human rights with the massacre in
Acteal. The same one of the massacres of El Charco and El Bosque.

That SCJN was the one that opposed relevant transformations that benefited the
people of Mexico during the term of former President López Obrador, such as
the Electricity Industry Law and the Hydrocarbons Law, and that, together with
former judge Juan Pablo Gómez Fierro –the one who granted amparos to companies
such as Ingemar–, judicialized reforms.

Norma Piña, who presided over the SCJN at the end of the previous stage, voted
for the unconstitutionality of the Federal Law of Republican Austerity, the
National Law of Asset Forfeiture and the Law of the National Public Security
System, and invalidated the electoral Plan B. In other words, she
systematically opposed democratization.

That previous Judicial Branch was the one that constantly released generators
of violence. A few examples are enough for the people of Mexico to remember
what kind of relationships it had: the Fifth Collegiate Court in
Administrative Matters gave Luis Cárdenas Palomino “the protection and shelter
of the justice of the Union” to unblock one of his accounts; the Seventeenth
Collegiate Court in Administrative Matters of the First Circuit of Mexico City
revoked the ruling of the Twelfth Court with which the amparo requested by the
wife of Genaro García Luna against her inclusion in the List of Blocked
Persons of December 9, 2019, had been denied; the Criminal Court of First
Instance of Hidalgo, in Guerrero, ordered on Wednesday, May 18, the immediate
release of Héctor Luis Palma Salazar, better known as el Güero.

### **Right-Wing Network Behind the Documentary**

Who are the organizations behind the documentary and why is it important for
the people of Mexico to know where they come from?

The Due Process of Law Foundation (DPLF) has been directed by Katya Salazar
since 2009. This foundation, the _think tank_ The Inter American Dialogue –the
same one that, during the term of Felipe Calderón, promoted the plan “Vision
2030: The Mexico We Want”– and the Mexican Bar Association carried out in 2024
the research “A Threat to Judicial Independence. Analysis of the Initiative of
Constitutional Reforms in Mexico.” Its authors were Adriana García, expert
adviser at the Rule of Law Impact Lab at Stanford Law School, and Daniel
Caballero, associate of the Rule of Law Program at the Inter-American
Dialogue. It was edited by Amrit Singh, professor of practice and executive
director of the Rule of Law Impact Lab at Stanford Law School, and Tamara
Taraciuk Broner, director of the Rule of Law Program at the Inter-American
Dialogue.

To present that document, a conference was held in February 2024 in which
Luisa Conesa Labastida, José Ramón Cossío, Úrsula Indacochea (of DPLF) and
Laurence Pantin (director of Juicio Justo), among others, participated.

![Acknowledgments page of the report](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/2026-11-11-right-wing-network-documentary-03-report-
acknowledgments.png)Image: Contralínea

The organization Juicio Justo has as its director Laurence Pantin, a member of
the collective “Justicia que Queremos” –which also opposed the judicial
reform–, who was general director of the Fundación para la Justicia and
coordinator of the Transparency in Justice program at México Evalúa, an
organization that opposed the judicial reform and the government of López
Obrador, and that **receives resources from the United States government, via
the coup-plotting National Endowment for Democracy (NED)**.

Alejandra Quezada also coincides at Juicio Justo as research coordinator. She
is a member of the International Open Justice Network and worked at the
Electoral Tribunal of the Federal Judicial Branch with former magistrate Reyes
Rodríguez Mondragón, an opponent of the Morena governments, protector of
opposition parties such as the PAN and the PRI. Like Pantin, she worked at
México Evalúa and collaborated with opposition media such as Nexos, Proceso
and Animal Político.

Lastly, the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung (KAS) is an organization that held
training courses with the previous SCJN, headed by Norma Piña, and also with
the National Action Party. It is **a German right-wing organization that has
extensive contacts with the international and Latin American right**.

In Mexico, the KAS has as allies the SCJN, the National Electoral Institute
(INE), the PAN, the Government of Guanajuato (which is governed by Acción
Nacional), the Government of Yucatán, that of Chihuahua, governed by María
Eugenia Campos, who opened the door to the CIA, and the city councils of
Chihuahua, Mérida and Puebla.

Among its partners it counts the NGO Prolocal, Hannover Fairs México, the
Mexican Association of International Studies (AMEI), El Toque, a multimedia
platform opposed to the government of Cuba, México Evalúa (which in turn
receives funding from the NED, the Atlas Network, Iniciativa Climática México,
Fundación Sertull, the Open Society Foundation, among others), the Institute
for Strategy and Research in Defense (ISDR), the Center for Political and
Social Studies (CEPOS), the Mexican Business Council for Foreign Trade,
Investment and Technology, the Employers’ Confederation of the Mexican
Republic (COPARMEX) and the Social Union of Mexican Entrepreneurs (USEM). And
in Venezuela, it also supports the opposition and coup-plotting Mesa de Unidad
de Acción Democrática (MUAD).

Locating the institutions behind the hoax and the propaganda that the
documentary “When We Lost Our Judgment” entails means knowing that it is a
right-wing power network that systematically opposed the delivery of social
justice. **The people did not lose their judgment; what they won was
justice.**
